Figure 1:FilmFlow at a glance.Cooperating agents use visual feedback to iteratively refine
executable camera plans, enabling text-directed camera generation
and reference-video directed camera generation in static or dynamic 3D scenes.

Figure 2:System design of FilmFlow.The Interpreter grounds
the instruction in the 3D scene; the Scout searches for an
opening viewpoint; the Director composes concurrent atomic operations
into a camera plan, optionally conditioned on a retrieved demonstration
(ICL). A shared Critic combines hard checks, visual assessment, and
temporal quality to guide both the Scout and Director.

Figure 3:Qualitative comparison for text-directed camera generation.The instruction and target 3D scene are shown on the left;
rows show each method’s output at the indicated timestamps.
While the baselines mostly show walls or obstructed views,
FilmFlow reveals the pedestrians, turns toward the boulevard,
and brings the target green sedan into view.

Figure 4:Qualitative comparison for video reference-directed camera generation.Reference frames and the target 3D scene are shown on the left;
rows on the right show each method’s output at the indicated
timestamps.
FilmFlow adjusts the viewpoint as the subject moves and keeps
the subject visible across the sampled frames.
LingBot-Map misses the subject in the opening frames,
VGGT-Ω\Omegacrops the subject in later frames,
and the zero-shot VLM loses the subject in the final frame.
The comparison concerns camera behavior rather than scene appearance.

Figure 5:Qualitative ablation for text-directed camera generation.FilmFlow shows close views of the red, green, and dark-clothed
characters before returning to the red character.
Without Scout, the opening remains a distant group view;
without Critic or ICL, foreground characters obstruct the
intended subject in intermediate frames.
The instruction and target scene are shown on the left;
columns show frames at the indicated timestamps.

Figure 6:Qualitative ablation for video reference-directed camera generation.FilmFlow maintains more consistent target framing across the
sampled frames, while the ablated variants show less consistent
subject scale, obstructed views, or loss of the target.
Reference frames and the target 3D scene are shown on the left;
columns show outputs at the indicated timestamps.

header: Appendix ATechnical Details of the Agentic System

images.caption:
Figure 7:Additional qualitative comparison for text-directed camera generation.
The instruction requests a bullet-time orbit that starts from a rear three-quarter view,
sweeps to the front of a crouching, backward-leaning figure, and settles into a locked-off hold.
The instruction and target 3D scene are shown on the left; rows show each method’s output at
the indicated timestamps. LAMP and GenDoP drift away from the figure toward the wall or empty
frames, and CinemaTraj approaches the figure but leaves it off-center under an oblique view.
FilmFlow keeps the figure centered as the rooftop slides behind it and ends on a stable frontal
view of the backbend.

Figure 8:Additional qualitative comparison for video reference-directed camera generation.
The reference clip moves from a view of the group toward a single subject and ends on a tight
close-up. Reference frames and the target 3D scene are shown on the left; rows show each
method’s output at the indicated timestamps. LingBot-Map stays close to a static wide view,
VGGT-Ω\Omegacrops the subject in intermediate frames, and the zero-shot VLM loses the subject
in the final frame. FilmFlow reproduces the progression from group view to single subject and
ends on a close-up that matches the reference framing. The comparison concerns camera behavior
rather than scene appearance.

Figure 9:An example of Scout refinement. The Director-specified opening (w/o Scout) and
the Scout-selected opening are shown for the same instruction, with the
Scout’s selection rationale and the corresponding camera states.
Elevation denotes the camera’s pitch angle; the Scout-selected camera
is placed higher and pitched downward toward the subject.

Figure 10:An example of Director refinement under a fixed opening.
Frame sequences and operation timelines before and after revision
show how Critic feedback guides changes to operation parameters
and temporal composition.

header: Appendix GApplication: Grey Model Reference as Video-Generation Conditions

Figure 12:Grey model render as a video-generation condition (group close-ups).The top row shows the grey model render of a FilmFlow trajectory that gives successive
close-ups to figures in a group. Each subsequent row is generated from the same render with
a different text prompt. Camera motion, framing, and subject placement follow the render,
while appearance follows the prompt.

Figure 13:Grey model render as a video-generation condition (leading shot).The top row shows the grey model render of a FilmFlow trajectory that leads two walking
subjects while other characters enter from the right. The four generated videos keep the
framing of the pair and the timing of the entering characters across different styles.
